name: peer-egress-socket-binding
notes: select: routes are candidates in table order; the answer is the interface of the route with the longest prefix containing the destination, then the lowest metric, then the first listed. Routes with usable false, and routes whose interface equals the tunnel, are not candidates. A null interface means the dial is refused.
An empty tunnel name leaves nothing out. A node without a TUN device has no tunnel routes to avoid.

windows: metric is the route's metric plus its interface's metric; usable is the interface having an IPv4 row that is connected, and not a 0.0.0.0/0 route on an interface with DisableDefaultRoutes. interface is the decimal interface index.

windows tables: a ULONG count, padding to offset 8, then fixed-size rows. Rows whose family is not AF_INET are skipped, as are forward rows with a prefix length over 32. A forward prefix is masked by its length. A buffer shorter than the count claims is refused whole.
macos: candidates are the rows of `netstat -rn -f inet` as the route vector normalises them; interface is the Netif column, metric is 0, and usable is the Flags column not containing I.

gateway: the route's next hop as an IPv4 address, or empty for on-link. Windows writes on-link as 0.0.0.0. On macOS the Gateway column is a gateway only on a route whose Flags contain G; otherwise it holds link#N, a MAC address, an interface name, or the address of a loopback or point-to-point peer, none of which is a hop.

linux: candidates are the lines of `ip -4 route show table main`. A leading blackhole, unreachable, prohibit or throw leads nowhere: the route stays a candidate with an empty interface. local, broadcast, anycast, multicast and nat lines are not read. A multipath route takes its first indented nexthop; one whose next hops cannot be read is not usable. dead is not usable; linkdown is. metric defaults to 0.
hops: the same choice as select, with owned prefixes also left out; a chosen route with an empty interface means no hop. Used for a bypass route when the platform's own query answers with the tunnel.

cases.name: default-only
cases.note: The common case: one physical default route and nothing else.

cases.name: tunnel-route-is-left-out
cases.note: The case the binding exists for. This node's own consumer rule sends 203.0.113.0/24 into the tunnel; the egress socket must take the default route instead.

cases.name: without-a-tunnel-the-tunnel-route-would-win
cases.note: The same table with no tunnel named, which is what makes the previous case load-bearing: leaving the tunnel out is the only thing that changes the answer.

cases.name: another-vpn-keeps-its-routes
cases.note: A route on some other interface -- a corporate VPN, a second NIC -- is not the tunnel and is respected, which binding everything to the default interface would break.

cases.name: prefix-length-beats-metric
cases.note: A longer prefix wins however large its metric is.

cases.name: equal-length-lower-metric-wins
cases.note: Two default routes, as on a laptop with both Ethernet and Wi-Fi up.

cases.name: equal-length-equal-metric-first-listed-wins
cases.note: A full tie keeps table order, so every runtime reading the same table agrees.

cases.name: unusable-route-is-left-out
cases.note: A route on a disconnected interface, or a scoped route on macOS, is not a candidate however good it looks.

cases.name: only-the-tunnel-leads-there
cases.note: No physical path. The dial is refused rather than left unbound, because unbound is exactly the socket that would follow the tunnel route.

cases.name: tunnel-name-match-is-exact
cases.note: utun30 is some other product's tunnel, not utun3.

cases.name: loopback-destination
cases.note: What the real-socket tests lean on: 127.0.0.1 resolves to the loopback interface, and a socket bound anywhere else cannot reach it.

cases.name: tunnel-owns-a-default-route
cases.note: Phase one refuses a 0.0.0.0/0 rule, but whatever routes the tunnel carries, they are left out the same way.

forwardTables.name: typical
forwardTables.note: A physical default route, loopback, this node's tunnel carrying a rule prefix and the mesh network, a disconnected Wi-Fi with a stale default, a VPN interface that disables default routes, another VPN's 10/8, and three rows that must not be read: an IPv6 row, a prefix length of 33, and a row whose address has host bits set, which is read masked.

forwardTables.name: truncated
forwardTables.note: The count says two rows and the buffer holds one. Reading the second would read past the allocation, so the whole table is refused.

interfaceTables.name: typical
interfaceTables.note: The interfaces of the typical forward table, plus an IPv6 row for an index that also has an IPv4 row; only the IPv4 one is read.

cases.name: rule-prefix-goes-out-the-physical-default
cases.note: Interface 9's default route has the best metric of the three but its interface disables default routes, and interface 15's is on a disconnected adapter, so the answer is 3.

cases.name: disable-default-routes-leaves-other-routes-usable
cases.note: The flag rules out interface 9's default route only; its 172.16.0.0/12 still carries traffic.

cases.name: mesh-network-route-is-left-out
cases.note: The forced-deny list refuses a mesh address before any dial; were one to get this far, it still would not be sent into the tunnel.

cases.name: masked-row-matches-its-network
cases.note: The row for interface 7 carries 10.1.2.3 with a length of 8. Read masked it is 10.0.0.0/8 and covers 10.200.0.1.

cases.name: linux-covered-address-goes-out-the-physical-default
cases.note: What `ip route get 203.0.113.9` could not answer: in the same namespace it said dev specus0. Of the two default routes the lower metric wins.

cases.name: linux-lower-metric-wins-between-equal-prefixes
cases.note: Printed metric 20 first, but the metric decides, not the order.

cases.name: linux-blackhole-leads-nowhere
cases.note: The default routes cover it too. The table deliberately does not reach it, so no bypass is pinned through them.

cases.name: linux-halves-over-the-default
cases.note: Two /1 routes into the tunnel cover everything; the /0 behind them is still there.

cases.name: macos-on-link-network-has-no-gateway
cases.note: The Gateway column says link#7, which is not a hop.

cases.name: macos-interface-route-has-no-gateway
cases.note: The Gateway column names lo0, which is not a hop either.

cases.name: windows-on-link-network-has-no-gateway
cases.note: Windows writes on-link as a next hop of 0.0.0.0.

cases.name: owned-bypass-is-left-out
cases.note: A bypass this feature installed earlier still names the gateway it was resolved to. Resolving again has to look past it, or a network change would keep the old hop.

windows.note: A four-byte value holding the interface index in network byte order. In host order setsockopt refuses it with WSAEADDRNOTAVAIL ("The requested address is not valid in its context").

macos.note: A four-byte int holding the interface index in host byte order, which is little-endian on every Mac this ships to.
